interactions.title: Tak leads the party to Nora
lines: DM: So, as you all walk following Tak, who is a youngish dwarf, maybe forty or so, for the— it looks like [garbled], dusty, without much of a beard, wearing patched and mended clothes that have been— that have been sewed and mended many, many times over. He moves with a sort of nervous energy, seeming almost younger than he looks, never still, never comfortable as he walks along the cliff, constantly glancing back to make sure you're following, rushing forward a bit, then rushing back, then rushing forward again.

DM: You can see now, after maybe an hour's walk or so in the distance ahead of you, a ghostly dwarf wearing full-plate armor, carrying a battle axe slung on her back, but insubstantial, ethereal, especially in the dim, flat light of this place, when she seems perched almost on, ah, on a rock outcropping, gazing intently south and east across the river, seemingly staring at the large, partially ruined statue of the huge stone warrior in the distance. She turns slowly as your group approach and looks at Tak, who squeaks, "They want to talk to you," before kind of quailing under her gaze, and then she turns, and she looks at you all, waiting for you to speak.

before: DM: So as you approach this ghost, why don't you all just briefly reintroduce your characters to everybody, so we remember— remember everybody. You want to go first?

Riswynn: Thank you. So Riswynn is heavily armored, carrying a warhammer, has in her possession a mystical cup. And, uh, she's been ah, enthusiastically, um, trying to figure out what's going on in this place since we got here, because it has always been her ah, intention to obey the gods and to fulfill their wills, and she finds herself in another situation where she's been tasked to um, follow their requests.

Rothfis: Last week, two weeks ago, you—you met Rothfis as well. He was a bartender, and he has been summoned to take over a debt owed by his ex-wife's clan, and he's not too pleased about it. Yeah, he's just trying to get through it and get back to the Stonefist Steins and Stables.

Thror: Thror Redpeak is a— dressed as a sailor, and is here, having just yesterday made a vow to turn his life around, if only we could go home again. Surprised to find um, the way home coming so soon, and so dressed in sailors clothes. It's—it's sparks playing around his fingers every so often.

Merash: You also met Merash Emberfoot a couple of weeks ago, who, while on her pilgrimage, had been stuck in a storm and survived, and having been saved from that, uh, led a quiet life of service, you, uh, and is now paying her penance for being saved. Um, she's fairly well armored, um, mostly has skills at a forge, and is not begrudgingly, but a little upset at having to come back and pay their price.
after: Unknown: You you!
Riswynn: I didn't even want to say anything.
DM: Do you want to discuss what you're planning on doing out of character first?
Unknown: Here.
Thror: Yeah, it's too funny. What are we planning on to make?

interactions.title: Nora recounts Hagrim’s fall and identifies Del
lines: Riswynn: Nora Silverspark, [garbled]. We are honored to meet you. We need to know more about this place where we find ourselves and the history of your party. I can— to show our mission, and so we ask you if you will tell us the tale of how you came to this place, and what does it mean to—what is a meaning of the current state of things where Morkalan is always watching? Everyone is trapped in the village of Bleakhold.
DM: She looks over you sort of coldly and says, "And what is your mission?"
Riswynn: We seek one who traveled, of course. We seek one who traveled with you when you first came here.
Rothfis: Hi! We're looking for Hagrim! What we heard in this is, you are all—

DM: What concern of yours is Hagrim and the ghosts of this place? There are a few outsiders here. I can see by your clothing that you have not spent long in this land. What business is of yours? What business is it of mine to aid you in this? It's—it—
Rothfis: Honestly, I couldn't give two cusses about him, but the Bahrâzel have me here to find Hagrim, so I must. My understanding is that you are the best we can do.
Riswynn: It is in the interest of justice and resolution.
DM: You are sent by the gods?
Rothfis: I— with ale aplenty if it pleases you.
Rothfis: I turn around to the rest, and I say, "I don't know if I trust her."
DM: Did not know the gods cared, at all for us. You said it is justice you seek. What sort of justice would you bring?
Riswynn: It depends on the right understanding of the situation.
DM: What do you want from me?

Riswynn: We cannot judge what we don't understand. We cannot serve justice to one we cannot find. If you have a tale of what this man has done, what this dwarf has done, or an inkling as to his present circumstances, that would be a great help to us.

DM: ((Persuasion check)) She looks at you, and she says, It was long ago. I don't— don't rightly know how we got here, exactly. I do not know that I— There are a few here who I would trust, but I will say this: I do not think this was Hagrim's fault.
DM: Yes, he snapped in battle, and has dwelled here long, now— created this place around his haunted memories.
Rothfis: What do you mean, he created it? He's— he's not Morkalan now, is he?
DM: It's what he calls himself.
Rothfis: Well, that makes for a different story altogether, I think.
Thror: What did happen then? What's the real story, as far as you can tell?
DM: Do not know why I should trust you. What will you do for us? What will you do for me?
Thror: What do you mean, this place?

DM: Do not know. It's been so long. She turns, and she sort of, and she looks at Tak. I was born here. I've never even heard the blessing of the gods or their names. We have been cut off for so long. You say that the gods sent you, but many have come before claiming to be sent by the gods. Why should we? Why should I trust? Why should I trust you?
Rothfis: Well, did any of them have a cup like that? Why, don't I— you're not interested in ale. Maybe you're interested in whatever she's offering.
DM: She looks, and she sort of turns slightly even more insubstantial. It survived. How? Thought sure, when the— when we lost the battle, the giant or the trolls would have destroyed that.

Riswynn: No, it ended, buried in the wreckage of that field of that battle, and was found ages later, and when I learned of its being found, our people sent me to reclaim it and bring it back to our— and— and home. But the gods took note that it was again amongst the dwarves, and sent it here for this use with us.
DM: She looks, um, kind of hungrily at the chalice.

DM: I guess I can share the story with you. If you bear the artifacts of the gods... It's, it's—it's— We left, I don't know how many years ago now—time passes strangely in this place— traveling with that very chalice, looking for refuge for those who had survived the Great War.

DM: Hagrim in those days was a seasoned veteran, fought mind flayers and worse, and the the deeps underneath the mountains. Happened to him there, because well, he didn't want to. He didn't want to go. He was reluctant to join our expedition. I think he was hoping maybe, for a heroic death. We found many refugees, turned south. Wounded but not defeated, fled with maybe five hundred dwarfs, hoping to lead them to safety.

DM: North of the human city of Tokra we encountered the son of a fire giant who had been slaughtered by the the humans. He called himself Mavdyrson. He was leading an army of trolls, and we were— We were trapped. We holed up. We built a fortification, hoping to outlast the giant. Think— I think we would have... Sort of pauses for a moment, and, like, her features become slightly indistinct.
DM: I was commanding the the flank of the war bands.

DM: Holding ground against the trolls while Hagrim and his elite squad of warriors attempted to take down the giant himself. You— I was young. It was my first battle. I ordered a retreat which turned into a rout. [garbled]! My—fled. Something in Hagrim snapped. I think he thought I had turned on the dwarfs, and that— think he thought he was betrayed again. Maybe— maybe the old horrors of the mind-altering evils of the great War came back to him, and he turned on me, and as we fought on the battlefield he ordered his troops to slay my companions. We would not fight back, and so we were slaughtered.
DM: He turned then, I believe, and killed everything around him in a rampage, and when I awoke well, I was in this place. Darkness grew, the domain of Morkalan, the land of the dishonored dead.

DM: And I have watched since then as he has turned, I don't know, ever more paranoid, angry. This place has gotten darker and darker, but I cannot leave this spot where I died. Nothing I can do. Do not think he can leave the site of his last battle, either, at the feet of that statue. I don't know if he even remembers anymore. Some are— Some say that the ghosts that haunt the ruined statue are Hagrim's memories made spirit.
DM: I know not what you or the gods will do with this information. That is what I can tell you.
Riswynn: We honor you for telling us your great and woeful tale.
Rothfis: So what— you're a ghost. What is Tak, then? What is Bleakhold? What— it is—this whole place is uh, a dreamscape?

DM: The best I can figure, the refugees who survived, were not killed in the slaughter, were drawn into this place. Possibly others have wandered in since. There, there's rumor of a few humans lurking around to— much younger than us, but as long as Morkalan—Hagrim— rules here, none can leave, and none can die.
Rothfis: We have to face him in battle. Is there anything we should know? Is he somehow, the—in a weakened state? Is there something that gives him power here?
DM: I believe he is a ghost like me. Normal weapons cannot hurt him. Only magic, enchanted items.
Rothfis: So when did he die?

DM: I don't know. After me. Do not know what happened from the— between the moment he slaughtered me on the battlefield, and the moment I woke here, but I know he did not slaughter all the dwarfs who were there, because some— some are now trapped here. I know he is not a living creature. Not anymore.
Thror: What does he want in all of this, I mean, does he want to be here? Does he want to be free? Does he want to die? What—
DM: I don't even think he remembers Hagrim anymore.
Thror: Do you know what Hagrim's home and the story was before you met him?
DM: I don't. I don't know much. He grew up in Ardith, the kingdom that fell in the Great War.
DM: He was always close with Del, his cousin, who was on the expedition with us. I don't know if he lived or died. He might be able to speak more of his childhood.
Riswynn: Tak, do you know Del?

DM: Del? Um, yeah. When I was—when I was very little, but that's who they call him, the mad priest, now. That used to be his name, Del Firebrand. He was was exiled by Morkalan, sent to the wastes. Nobody knows if he's alive or dead.
Riswynn: But he was telling stories of the places you were all from. If I recall your {{neighborhoods fathers tales}}.
Thror: How would you find a person in the wastes?

DM: Well, um! This is Tak speaking. I I don't go in the wastes. There's trolls there. Hagrim controls—Morkalan controls them. That's where those who— well, if you displease Morkalan, that's where you're sent, and everybody says the trolls eat your spirit.
DM: I—I guess. I—I mean, I wouldn't go there, but I'm not strong like you.
Riswynn: There's some wisdom in choosing your battles, Tak.

Thror: And choosing battles you can survive, especially. Address the ghost again, and—and there's no way out? You—you spoke of people who had come. Where, where did they go? And where did the humans come from? I mean, people just show up here from time to time, then?
DM: Indeed, I think those who wander into the ruins wander onto the battlefield.
Thror: But never the other way around?
DM: Never the other way around. Perhaps with powerful magic.
Unknown: And you don't hear the gods here, then?
DM: No! Those who die stay. Even death is not an escape.
Rothfis: Getting your spirit eaten by a troll an escape?
Rothfis: Just sit in a belly for the rest of time?
DM: Or maybe— maybe you become a troll.

before: Unknown: Bye.
Riswynn: I will, yes, go ask her.
Unknown: You.
Riswynn: I will say, "We greet you. Tak has told us that we are in the presence of..." Insert name here. I'm really doing badly with names right now.
DM: Nora, Nora Silverspark.
after: Thror: And one of the humans—does anyone know why they're here, what they're doing here? Why they ended up...
Riswynn: I believe that they were looking for the Chalice of the Runepriest.
Thror: Uh! And then wandered into the battlefield, presumably.
Riswynn: Mhm.
Unknown: Humans.

interactions.title: The chalice’s healing and refuge legends
lines: DM: ((Personal teleport-token rules)) The chalice, however, who knows what it can do? It is clearly like a divine artifact, and the stories and legends around it are all about sort of healing and refuge and safety. Reason they, the dwarves, brought it to go look for refugees is because it was supposed to have like magic healing powers.
Riswynn: But my entire expertise in wielding this magic item is touching it or not, and—
DM: Attempting to teleport you and your companions to safety, and only teleporting you.
DM: So who knows how to actually use it? Or if you can even actually use it.

before: Riswynn: I think succeeding in our task is our ticket home.
DM: So you do all have those like slivers of whatever that let you teleport, should you fail and decide to give up, you—
Thror: I forgot about this, Tim. All right. Remind me, Like, when we started down the path, we just, like, had those sort of things?

DM: Yeah, before you walked into here. The idea of the—the primary purpose being, like, the— they teleport you back to where you were before the quest is done. But the secondary purpose being, you fail, you're not necessarily trapped here forever.
Thror: Do we know, sort of mechanically, are those tuned to us, have, like, fingerprint locks on them? Or could we give that to somebody else?
after: Rothfis: So, are we contemplating going to see the humans, then?
Thror: I'd rather— I agree, because if the humans went looking for the chalice and we have the chalice.
Rothfis: The—because when I was in [garbled]—
Thror: Yeah, if we don't want to give it up, it might be a fight.
Rothfis: I don't know if they've got much to—

interactions.title: Rothfis wants his obligation to the Ironhorns severed
lines: Rothfis: ((Route planning)) If I don't do this right, the Ironhorns are going to continue to pester me for the rest of time, and I'd rather that this was properly severed. I don't want any more, "Oh, but can we just talk about this?" No.

before: Thror: Well, where to? Then? The waste?
Rothfis: You know. Let me hear it. It's not the wastes I meant, and I'm not the ghost, neither. Should I take a vote?

Riswynn: I wouldn't say that I'm advocating that we should scour the wastes for weeks at a time, looking for this traveler. But if we can make our way slightly, roundaboutly towards the confrontation with Hagrim, perhaps fortuitously run into the traveler, the mad priest on the way, I'd rather do that than make a bee line for the battle.
Rothfis: You'd rather maybe bump into a spirits eating troll along the way.
Riswynn: I'm more worried about facing Hagrim unprepared, and not being able to complete our mission than having to fight a troll.
after: DM: So.
Thror: Well, let's let's not waste any time.
DM: Okay. So where are you going? Somebody has just got to make a decision. You're currently somewhat north of the statue.
Merash: Sounds like we're going to the statue, but in a roundabout way. We kind of into the waste a bit.

DM: Okay, uh. So are you heading like straight across the river and then turn south, or you're gonna circle back to Bleakhold and then cross and head north like the— here are the— ah, let me draw a little map. And okay. So basically you've got.

interactions.title: Tak is escorted toward Bleakhold
lines: Riswynn: Do we make sure that Tak’s Okay, getting back to Bleakhold safely?
Riswynn: I mean, he's gone back and forth a bit, few times. Maybe he's confident that he won't get into—it won't end up holed up in another—
DM: I mean. He certainly would not object to the company if you were willing to escort him back closer to Bleakhold. He's not going to insist on it.

Merash: I think if we go back to Bleak and then cross, then we at least get like more of a fair trek through the wastelands back to the shadow—or to the statue, and then we can also make sure that Tak’s home okay.

DM: Okay. So you turn south and head back in the direction of Bleakhold with Tak, stopping a little bit short of where the sort of zombie guards are sort of pacing around ((River crossing and landscape))

before: DM: Okay, uh. So are you heading like straight across the river and then turn south, or you're gonna circle back to Bleakhold and then cross and head north like the— here are the— ah, let me draw a little map. And okay. So basically you've got.
Unknown: This is terrible.
DM: You've got the river. You've got Bleakhold. There, you've got the statue.
Unknown: Oh, come on.

DM: You got the statue, like, there. You are currently, like, here, so you could go. You could go like across the river here and like, wander through and come south, or you could go back across the—over here and turn north. You could just go straight south and cross the river right where the statue is.
after: Unknown: Um!

DM: It's sort of dry and dusty. Everything is sort of obscured by the dust. There's a faint—even though there's not really—you can't really feel a wind. It's like as if there was a wind blowing up dust. So everything was considered lightly obscured, so it's hard to see much.
DM: Um! What is your—you're just gonna, like, wander around? You have direction you want to head? Scouting plan? Trying to be stealthy?

Merash: Well, I don't think myself or Riswynn will ever be stealthy, but I wouldn't mind trying to look around a little bit and see if there's any sort of like waypoints, or any sort of finger posts, or anything that might give us a sense of direction through the waste lands.
DM: There. Okay, Um.

interactions.title: Del remembers Hagrim, their lost home and the war
lines: DM: You begin to approach, and you hear this kind of um, noise that sounds like rocks falling and something walking in. You turn, like, holding your war hammer, until you hear a voice, and from it emerges, "Hey! Who's there?"
Riswynn: I say, "Riswynn Brawnanvil of the Ardith Mountains."

DM: What are you doing here? You see, like, kind of beginning, like, peering out from the cave, this, like, old dwarf, like, leaning on a staff, um, long, dusty, unkempt white beard, kind of squinting a little bit, like walks a little bit forward, and like taps your armor with his staff. There's one.
Riswynn: Indeed! That's what you want. Me. I'd like to hear some tales of the past.
DM: Hmm! Isn't it—ah, which past?
Riswynn: Your past. I can't— before this bleak realm.
DM: Sun. Walks forward a little bit and kind of peers up into the sky. You— not out today? No.
DM: Come, sit. Yeah, they can. They have caught up. It kind of looks—looks out. More Riswynns.
DM: Yeah, he looks alive. I mean, he's old, but he's probably past two hundred.
Rothfis: Yeah, I'll uh I'll offer him a pint. Then, of course.

DM: Kind of sits down, and he's like there's a you know. You can see he's sort of pushed some rocks around the bottom of the cave to try and make what looks kind of like a like a house of sorts. Sort of taps a chair. Riswynn, sit, Riswynn, and he looks over at Rothfis for you, Riswynn.
Rothfis: Ah, yeah, thanks very much. That's quite quite kind of you. The best seat in the house I can see. Well, I've got the best pint of ale you've had in. Well, probably a hundred years, I bet.
DM: And he kind of reaches over and he he takes a sip and he— to me. I remember the brewery I'm in there, in the city where I grew up.
Rothfis: Well, actually, my—that's my clan, Stonefist.
DM: It is um wait, Bronze. Kind of shakes his head. Yeah, Hagrim and I used to go sit there and talk about.
DM: Great adventures we'd have, my hand. The finest— what is that, um, bone with meat around it? You roast from a lamb?
DM: Hmm. First, spit, at the finest roast spit. I used to sit— drinks another sip of the beer, says, "Ah, this is good."
Rothfis: Well, I should hope so. I brew it myself.
DM: He looks, right, who are you? He looks at Thror. What? Where did you come from?
Thror: I came in with the Riswynns. I’m Thror.
DM: Thror. Riswynn. Hmm. Nice to meet you.
Thror: Good to meet you, too. Someone told me you were dead right?
Thror: No, you drink like a live dwarf.
Rothfis: Okay, you're spilling all the ale.
DM: Maybe—maybe maybe you're dead, too.
Rothfis: I think I was nearly dead about five minutes ago.

DM: Pokes at you again. Ah, Stonewind can't be dead. Taps right, like, taps with his stick on Merash's armor, and it's like pling, pling, pling, and, like, starts, like, trying to play a tune on your armor. [garbled] the bells, the center of the city. We had the bells that would play in the morning, and the night. Last— must have been a hundred of them. I always loved that sound. We're at— How are you?
Merash: I am Merash, Riswynn of the bells.
DM: Where Where did Where did you all come from? Where? What are you doing here?
Merash: We came to find you.
DM: Me, I I thought I was dead. Takes another sip of ale. Taps on the cask, now taps on the stone.
DM: He holds out his mug.
DM: Takes another sip. I should have never. We should have never gone.
Thror: What did you think would happen?

DM: Let’s get it. Where did you all come from? The— Where's where's Hagrim? Where's Nora? Where's—where's the army? We left just just a few weeks ago, heading north. I— I was— convinced Hagrim to go. He— He came back from the war. Changed. Um.

DM: Um takes another sip, um, thought it would be a great heroic fight that maybe maybe if we could see the great halls of our home one more time. I mean, Tharn Todor so primitive, almost nothing there. I don't know. Maybe it's changed now. Takes another sip. Kind of stares off.

DM: It all started going wrong. We found the city, but it was changed. It was dark. The great crystal lights that floated in the caverns, the waterfalls that poured from the cliffs into the river that— all dry. What— looks around—what— we are. This cave doesn't—this doesn't look right. Where are we? We have— Who are you? Where— where is this place the so dark?
Thror: What happened on the battlefield that day?
DM: Don't—don't— don't—don't remember. Don't— it's a—there's a— there was no battle.
DM: We didn't fight in the city. It was empty, it was— it was dark, it was black, it was washed away of all color. The farmers were gone. Wasn't the same.
Riswynn: It was not a home you could go back to. But did you find refugees to take away?

DM: They took us away. Hagrim took us away. [garbled]. He took us somewhere. Where did it— where did we go? Where did— looks around, like, taps on that, tries to, like, stand up, and he's, like, sort of wobbles a little bit. It kind of slips and reaches out and grabs onto Riswynn's armor and sort of propping himself up and looks around. Where did he? Where are we taken? Where am I?

Rothfis: From what we've heard, this might just be some sort of dream that Hagrim is having or pocket dimension. We're in a big old bag of holding that's just turned dark from his memories. Maybe some cheese would help yours, and I'll—I'll give them some of the same cheese I've been handing out.

DM: It takes a little bite. Who are you? It looks around at— Where did you come from? What? What? What are you doing here? It's not—it's different. It's not— they're not from here. They're not— stranger—strangers in this place. What— does Hagrim know? Looks straight at ah, Rothfis. Does Hagrim know? Did he send you?

Rothfis: I think he knows, because a patrol went to tell him we were here. But no, he didn't send us. We're here to meet him at some point, but wanted to get a sense of who he was from those that knew him before. I'm from Chardon. You remember that town, that city?
DM: Yes, Hagrim talked about Chardon, and he fought with the Mages in the Great War. We would— after the war, we would sit sometimes in the.

DM: Looking out over the plains up in the mountains, ah, well, Tharn Todor was being built, and look across, and he would talk about the magic— it's goddamn bad— evil that would devour your brains and replace it with some beast that would pilot your body. But it would not be you. It would be some something else that had devoured your mind, tentacled horrors.
DM: Like humans, but but not— no, it's just tentacles. He said he saw one grab one of the most powerful mages he knew, and just suck its brain out.
DM: They would burn in the fires, just like everything.
Rothfis: So so Hagrim might have met one of these tentacled horrors, and maybe that's why he turned. Maybe that's why a great dwarf and hero would do something so foul.
DM: He kind of goes still for a moment. His eyes were different when he came back, and he never once talked about the bells. It's like he forgot them.
Thror: Do you think there's something else inside him, piloting his body, then?
DM: I don't know about these things. Who are you? He looks around kind of scared. Where did you come from? What— What are you doing here? Did Hagrim send you?
Riswynn: We were sent? He turned on the room.

DM: We were fighting with Nora, and our line broke. The trolls got through, and he turned on us right at the moment when when a hero could have turned the tide, he turned on us. The look. It was not a dwarf looking out of his eyes.
DM: Who are you? What? Where did you come? Where am I?
Rothfis: Del? Would you like another pint? We're friends.
DM: Right, there's there's ale here.
Rothfis: Look in your hand, mate.
DM: He's, like, shaking, looks down.
Rothfis: Best trick I can do. I— I cheers them and—and drink from my cup, and—
DM: Hagrim didn't send you. Then why are you here?
Thror: We could rest here for the hour at least. Safe in the cave. Maybe.
Riswynn: Yeah, the cave should be safe.
DM: Yes, trolls, but they don't— they don't come here. Hagrim, um, he—he knows me, I think. We were friends once. Trolls don't come here.
Thror: When he told the stories of the tentacled monsters from the deep, did he ever tell you how to kill them?
DM: Oh, how, um, he said, fire, and bash their brains in.
Rothfis: Well, I can do the second.

DM: I don't know how many he killed. It sounded like there were armies in the deep. Not many came back from those fights. That's why we fled. Wasn't safe. Could never have killed them all. Collapse the tunnels, them down there, bury the long roads, flee the kingdom. Never wanted to flee, could have just fighting, but after the war he he was different.
DM: He looks down where he takes a sip of his ale. I am tired.

before: Unknown: Um!
Riswynn: I can do a third level Cure Wounds.
Rothfis: Thank you.
Riswynn: Right now, I'm going to re-roll perception. It's going to be—
Rothfis: Yeah [garbled]. Here.
after: Thror: Let’s rest.
DM: Go ahead and short rest. Um, Uh, Riswynn, you can get back, uh—
Riswynn: I was just looking at that, and I Channel Divinity.
DM: So you can use your Channel Divinity to get back spell slots.
Riswynn: Why not spend it?

interactions.title: What the party can expect from Hagrim’s ghost
lines: DM: ((Verbal scaffolding)) if he's undead, then whatever happened like, there's not a—a mind flayer can't— brain parasite can't possess the undead, right? It, like, it can take over the body of somebody. It could make them do all sorts of bad things, but once he's dead like, that's it. Like, if this is, like, the soul of the Hagrim trapped in this land, there's not— I—I mean, it's— in any case, it should—it should be clear, like, if there's a— there's no way that a parasite can hide in the skull of a ghost. Right? Yeah, there's going to be some, like, thing glommed on to the brain of the ghost, like, possessing its soul, or there's not.
Rothfis: But I—I had—I had sort of come to the hypothesis that, like, the fact that this plane exists is—is somehow related to the possession and the mind flayer. But perhaps that's incorrect.
